His CPA Daughter Says It's Time To Rethink Their $1.6M IRA Strategy
 Image via Shutterstock Caroline Lubinsky Wed, October 21, 2026 at 6:00 PM MST 11 min read Benzinga and Yahoo Finance LLC may earn commission or revenue on some items through the links below. 
 A 68-year-old retired operations manager and his 66-year-old wife have $1.6 million in traditional IRAs and pay their financial adviser about $16,000 a year to manage their portfolio. Over Labor Day weekend, their daughter, a CPA, looked at their tax returns and asked why they had never considered Roth conversions during the years since he retired. 
 He told her she was "second-guessing a professional." 
 His daughter has a question worth exploring. The years after retirement but before required minimum distributions begin can create an opportunity to convert some traditional IRA savings to a Roth IRA while taxable income is relatively low. But whether that makes sense depends on how much they convert, what tax rate they pay now, their future income and their plans for the money.

 With $1.6 million in traditional IRAs, the couple could benefit from reviewing the strategy before their RMDs begin. That doesn't mean they should convert hundreds of thousands of dollars without running the numbers. 
 Why Can The Years Before RMDs Matter? 
 The couple lives on savings in a taxable brokerage account, so their taxable income may be relatively low. If that leaves room in a lower tax bracket, they could consider converting a portion of their traditional IRA savings to a Roth IRA. 
 For 2026, married couples filing jointly can have up to $211,400 in taxable income before entering the 24% federal income tax bracket. The standard deduction is $32,200, though their actual taxable income depends on all their income and deductions. The IRS's 2026 tax figures provide the applicable thresholds. 
 A Roth conversion moves money from a traditional IRA into a Roth IRA. The untaxed portion converted is generally included in taxable income for the year of the conversion. The IRS explains the rules for Roth conversions. 
 The potential advantage is paying tax on some retirement savings now, possibly at a lower rate than the rate that would apply to future withdrawals. But the conversion itself increases taxable income, so a large conversion can push some of their income into a higher bracket or affect other income-based costs. 
 What Happens If They Do Nothing? 
 Their traditional IRAs can continue growing tax-deferred, but they will eventually have to take required minimum distributions. Under current rules, traditional IRA owners generally must begin RMDs at age 73. His first RMD year will depend on when he turns 73, and his wife's timeline is separate because she is two years younger. 
 Story Continues The size of future RMDs depends on the account balance at the end of the preceding year and the applicable IRS distribution period. For illustration, an account balance of $2 million divided by a distribution period of roughly 26.5 would produce an RMD of about $75,000. The actual amount will depend on his age and account balance when distributions begin. The IRS's RMD guidance explains how the calculation works. 
 Those withdrawals generally count as taxable income. If the couple also receives Social Security, pension income or other taxable income, their RMDs could push more of their income into higher tax brackets. 
 A Roth conversion can reduce the balance in a traditional IRA and potentially lower future RMDs. But the couple needs to weigh that potential benefit against the tax they would pay on the conversion today.

 Who Could Face A Bigger Tax Bill Later? 
 A surviving spouse is one consideration. When one spouse dies, the survivor may eventually have to file as single, with narrower tax brackets than those available to a married couple filing jointly. A similar amount of retirement income can therefore produce a higher tax bill after a spouse dies. 
 Their children may also inherit traditional IRA assets. Most non-spouse beneficiaries who inherit an IRA after the original owner's death generally must empty the account within 10 years, subject to exceptions. Withdrawals from an inherited traditional IRA are generally taxable, and distributions during those years can add to a beneficiary's other income. 
 For 2026, the 32% federal tax bracket for single filers begins at $201,775 in taxable income. That doesn't mean their children would automatically pay 32% on an inherited IRA: their other income, filing status and withdrawal timing would determine the actual tax rate. 
 Converting some assets to a Roth IRA could provide more flexibility for the couple or their heirs. Qualified Roth IRA distributions are generally tax-free, although inherited Roth IRAs are still subject to distribution rules. 
 How Much Could A Conversion Strategy Save? 
 The answer depends on the tax rate they pay on the conversion compared with the rate that would otherwise apply to withdrawals later. 
 For a simplified example, converting $100,000 entirely at a 22% marginal federal rate would generate about $22,000 in federal income tax. If the same amount would otherwise have been withdrawn later and taxed entirely at 32%, the federal tax on that withdrawal would be about $32,000. 
 That $10,000 difference illustrates the potential benefit of a lower tax rate today. It is not a guaranteed saving: a conversion may span multiple tax brackets, future rates can change, and the couple may have other tax consequences to consider. 
 Converting $100,000 annually for five years would move $500,000 before investment growth into a Roth IRA. But they should not assume that amount is the right target. A tax projection can help them identify how much they might convert each year without creating an unnecessarily large current tax bill. 
 If possible, paying the conversion tax from taxable savings rather than withholding it from the converted retirement funds can leave more money in the Roth IRA. They should also consider the effect on investment gains, cash reserves and other financial goals. 
 Could Roth Conversions Increase Medicare Premiums? 
 They could. Medicare uses income information from prior tax returns to determine whether beneficiaries pay income-related monthly adjustment amounts, or IRMAA, on Medicare Part B and Part D premiums. For 2026 premiums, the threshold for married couples filing jointly is $218,000 in modified adjusted gross income, based generally on their 2024 tax return. The Social Security Administration explains how IRMAA works .

 That $218,000 threshold is for 2026 premiums, not a guaranteed threshold for 2028. A Roth conversion completed in 2026 would generally affect the income used to determine 2028 Medicare premiums, when the applicable thresholds may be different. 
 This is why a conversion should be modeled against more than the federal income tax brackets. A move that appears efficient based on the marginal tax rate alone could also increase Medicare premiums or affect other income-sensitive provisions. 
 Is The Adviser At Fault? 
 Not necessarily. Some advisers primarily manage investments, while comprehensive tax planning may be provided separately or coordinated with a client's accountant. The couple should first establish what their adviser agreed to do. 
 Still, paying about $16,000 a year makes it reasonable to ask what planning services are included and whether the adviser has evaluated their retirement tax strategy. The firm's Form CRS relationship summary describes services, fees and conflicts. 
 They can ask the adviser to work with their daughter on a year-by-year tax projection that compares different conversion amounts, future RMDs, Medicare premiums and potential estate outcomes. If tax planning is outside the current engagement, they can ask about the cost of adding it or seek another opinion. 
 What Should They Do Before December 31? 
 Roth conversions generally must be completed by Dec. 31 to count for that tax year. The couple still has time to evaluate a 2026 conversion, but they should not rush into one simply to meet the deadline. 
 They should work with their CPA and adviser to estimate their taxable income, identify how much room remains in their preferred tax bracket and model how different conversion amounts could affect Medicare premiums and future RMDs. They should also decide where the tax payment would come from and whether it would leave enough money available for other needs. 
 Finance Advisors can connect them with a financial adviser focused on tax planning , including how Roth conversions, retirement withdrawals and Medicare costs fit together. 
 The key question isn't whether every retiree should convert traditional IRA savings to a Roth. It's whether this couple can use their current tax situation to make a better long-term decision — before required distributions begin and their options change.

 Building Wealth Across More Than Just The Market 
 Building a resilient portfolio means thinking beyond a single asset or market trend. Economic cycles shift, sectors rise and fall, and no one investment performs well in every environment. That's why many investors look to diversify with platforms that provide access to real estate, fixed-income opportunities, precious metals, and even self-directed retirement accounts. By spreading exposure across multiple asset classes, it becomes easier to manage risk, capture steady returns, and create long-term wealth that isn't tied to the fortunes of just one company or industry. 
 EquityMultiple 
 For accredited investors looking beyond stocks and bonds, EquityMultiple provides access to vetted commercial real estate deals starting at $5,000 , with only ~5% of opportunities passing their due diligence process. 
 Arrived 
 Backed by Jeff Bezos, Arrived Homes makes real estate investing accessible with a low barrier to entry. Investors can buy fractional shares of single-family rentals and vacation homes starting with as little as $100 . This allows everyday investors to diversify into real estate, collect rental income, and build long-term wealth without needing to manage properties directly. 
 Skybound Entertainment 
 Entertainment franchises can become valuable long-term assets when they successfully expand across multiple platforms. Skybound Entertainment, the company behind The Walking Dead and Invincible, develops original intellectual property that spans comics, television, film, video games, merchandise, and licensing . With more than 250 IPs in its portfolio and a strategy focused on retaining franchise rights while scaling successful stories across media, Skybound offers investors exposure to the growing entertainment and creator economy through a private company rather than traditional public market investments. 
 American PowerGen 
 As artificial intelligence drives a surge in electricity demand, reliable power generation is becoming a critical part of the technology ecosystem. American PowerGen is developing natural gas-fired power plants in Texas, a fast-growing market fueled by AI data centers, manufacturing expansion, and population growth. By advancing projects through permitting, fuel supply, and grid interconnection, the company is positioning itself to help meet rising energy needs while offering investors exposure to the infrastructure supporting the next wave of AI and industrial growth. 
 Bito 
 As AI coding tools take on more of the work traditionally done by developers, companies are facing new challenges around code quality, context and the rising cost of AI-powered development. Bito is building software designed to help AI coding agents better understand complex codebases while helping companies control AI development costs. Founded by former PubMatic executives, Bito has raised more than $10 million from institutional and individual investors and is now raising additional capital through a Wefunder offering, giving investors an opportunity to invest in a company targeting an emerging need within the rapidly expanding AI software market. 
 DLP Capital 
 For accredited investors looking beyond stocks and traditional real estate opportunities, DLP Capital provides access to private real estate strategies focused on workforce housing — homes for essential workers such as teachers, nurses, firefighters, and police officers. With more than $5.5 billion in assets under management and a community of 4,000+ accredited investors, DLP Capital gives investors access to real estate strategies designed around the growing need for housing that working Americans can actually afford. 
 FarmTogether 
 Farmland has historically held its value through market volatility and delivered returns uncorrelated to stocks and bonds. For accredited investors, FarmTogether offers direct access to high-quality U.S. farmland starting at $15,000 — fully managed, with no landlord headaches. 
 Fundrise 
 Private real estate and private credit can add income and stability to a stock-heavy portfolio. Fundrise offers access to diversified private real estate and credit strategies through an easy-to-use platform, with professionally managed portfolios designed to generate passive income and long-term growth.
